title: Big-O Notation
author: Bachmann, Landau
description: Big-O describes how an algorithm's cost grows as the input gets large.
hook: Two programs sort your photos. One is fine for 100 photos and chokes on 100,000. Same task, wildly different scaling. Big-O is how we predict that before it happens.
hook_action: Drag the input size n and watch how different growth rates pull apart.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag n, the input size, upward.
lessons_data.hint: Find n and drag it to the right.
lessons_data.insight: At small n almost any algorithm feels instant. The differences only show up as n grows.

lessons_data.instruction: Push n past 50.
lessons_data.insight: O(n²) work grows with the square of the input — doubling n quadruples the work. That is why nested loops get dangerous.

lessons_data.instruction: Take n all the way to its maximum.
lessons_data.insight: O(log n) barely moves while O(n²) explodes. Big-O ignores constants and keeps only the dominant term — because at scale, that is all that matters.

glossary_data.tooltip: Order of growth — the upper bound on how cost scales

title: Binary Search
author: John Mauchly
description: Halving the search space each step finds an item in a sorted list astonishingly fast.
hook: Guess my number between 1 and 1000. Guess randomly and you could take 1000 tries. Always guess the middle and you will win in at most 10. That is binary search.
hook_action: Drag the array size n and watch how few steps log₂(n) really is.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag n, the size of the sorted array.
lessons_data.insight: Each comparison throws away half of what is left. The worst case is the number of halvings: log₂(n).

lessons_data.instruction: Set n to 1024.
lessons_data.insight: 1024 items need only 10 comparisons. Double the data to 2048 and you add just one step. Logarithmic growth is the next best thing to free.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag n back down near 16.
lessons_data.insight: For tiny inputs a plain linear scan is just as fast and simpler. Binary search earns its keep on large, sorted data.

glossary_data.tooltip: Binary search only works on pre-sorted data
Each comparison throws away half of what's left
Doubling the list adds just one more step

title: Master Theorem
author: Bentley, Haken, Saxe
description: A recipe for the running time of divide-and-conquer algorithms.
hook: Merge sort splits a list in two, sorts each half, then merges. How fast is that? The Master Theorem reads the answer straight off the recursion.
hook_action: Drag a (how many subproblems) and b (how much smaller each one is).

lessons_data.instruction: Drag a — the number of subproblems each split creates.
lessons_data.insight: More subproblems means more work flows down the recursion tree. a and b together decide who wins: the splitting or the combining.

lessons_data.instruction: Set a = 2 and b = 2 (merge sort).
lessons_data.hint: Use the Merge sort preset or set a=2, b=2.
lessons_data.insight: With a = b the work is balanced at every level, giving the classic O(n log n).

lessons_data.instruction: Push a up to 7 (Strassen's matrix trick).
lessons_data.insight: Strassen multiplies matrices with 7 subproblems instead of 8, dropping the exponent below the naive O(n³). Tiny changes in a reshape the whole running time.

glossary_data.tooltip: a — how many subproblems each split creates
b — the factor each subproblem shrinks by
Cost of a problem written in terms of its smaller copies

title: Bayes' Theorem
author: Thomas Bayes
description: How to update a belief when new evidence arrives.
hook: A test for a rare disease is 99% accurate and you test positive. Are you doomed? Probably not — and Bayes' theorem shows why the base rate dominates.
hook_action: Drag the prior, the test sensitivity, and the false-positive rate.

variables_data.name: prior
variables_data.description: Prior — how common the condition is

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the prior P(A) upward.
lessons_data.insight: The prior is how common the condition is before any test. When it is tiny, even a positive result usually means a false alarm.

lessons_data.instruction: Push the prior up to about 0.3.
lessons_data.insight: As the condition becomes common, a positive test becomes much more trustworthy. Evidence is only as strong as the base rate it updates.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the false-positive rate down toward 0.
lessons_data.insight: Cutting false positives is what makes a test convincing for rare conditions. This is the base-rate fallacy that fools doctors, juries, and spam filters alike.

glossary_data.tooltip: Belief before seeing the evidence

title: Gradient Descent
author: Augustin-Louis Cauchy
description: Walk downhill on the error surface to train a model.
hook: Training a neural network is just rolling a ball downhill toward the lowest error. Step too small and it crawls; step too big and it bounces out of the valley.
hook_action: Drag the learning rate α and the starting point θ.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the learning rate α.
lessons_data.insight: α controls how far you move against the gradient each step. It is the single most important knob in training.

lessons_data.instruction: Set α to about 0.3.
lessons_data.insight: A well-chosen rate slides smoothly to the minimum in a few steps. This is the sweet spot every optimizer hunts for.

lessons_data.instruction: Now push α above 1.0.
lessons_data.insight: Too large a step overshoots the valley and the error grows instead of shrinks — the model diverges. Picking α is a balance between speed and stability.

glossary_data.tooltip: α — how far you step against the gradient
Slope of the error surface; it points uphill
The lowest-error point training is hunting for

title: Softmax
author: John S. Bridle
description: Turns a vector of scores into a probability distribution.
hook: A classifier outputs raw scores: cat 2.0, dog 1.0, bird 0.0. Softmax turns those into clean probabilities that sum to 100% — the language models speak.
hook_action: Drag the three logits and watch one win the probability mass.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag z₁, the score for the first class.
lessons_data.insight: Softmax exponentiates each score, so even a small lead in z₁ grabs a big share of the probability.

lessons_data.instruction: Set all three logits equal (try the Uniform preset).
lessons_data.hint: Use the Uniform preset, or set z₁=z₂=z₃.
lessons_data.insight: Equal scores give equal probabilities — here, 33% each. With no information, softmax spreads belief evenly.

lessons_data.instruction: Push z₁ up to 5 while the others stay low.
lessons_data.insight: A large gap makes softmax nearly one-hot: class 1 takes almost all the probability. Temperature scaling tunes exactly how sharp this gets.

glossary_data.tooltip: Raw, unnormalised class scores
Softmax turns scores into probabilities summing to 1
Exponentiating makes the largest score dominate

title: Cross Entropy
author: Claude Shannon
description: The loss that punishes a model for confident wrong answers.
hook: A model says it is 99% sure the image is a cat. It is a dog. Cross-entropy loss makes that mistake hurt — a lot. Confidence is only rewarded when it is right.
hook_action: Drag q, the probability the model assigned to the correct answer.

variables_data.name: q
variables_data.description: Predicted probability of the true class

lessons_data.instruction: Drag q, the probability the model gave the correct class.
lessons_data.insight: Cross-entropy loss is -log(q). The closer q is to 1, the smaller the loss.

lessons_data.instruction: Push q up toward 1.
lessons_data.insight: When the model is confidently correct, the loss approaches zero. This is the target every training step is reaching for.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag q down near 0.
lessons_data.insight: Confident and wrong is the worst case — the loss shoots toward infinity. That steep penalty is exactly what pushes the model to calibrate its confidence.

glossary_data.tooltip: q — the probability the model assigned
Penalty that grows as confident answers go wrong
−log q: how surprised the model is by the truth

title: Attention
author: Vaswani et al.
description: The mechanism that lets transformers decide what to focus on.
hook: When you read "the animal didn't cross the street because it was tired", you know "it" means the animal. Attention is how a transformer learns to look back at the right word.
hook_action: Drag the key dimension d_k and the match score to see why we divide by √d_k.

variables_data.name: score
variables_data.description: Raw match score between a query and a key

lessons_data.instruction: Drag d_k, the dimension of the query and key vectors.
lessons_data.insight: Dot products of longer vectors get larger just from having more terms. d_k measures that length.

lessons_data.instruction: Push d_k up to 512.
lessons_data.insight: Without scaling, large d_k makes the scores huge, softmax saturates, and gradients vanish. Dividing by √d_k keeps the scores in a sane range — the trick that made deep transformers trainable.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the match score QKᵀ up and down.
lessons_data.insight: A high score means this query strongly matches this key, so softmax sends more weight to that value V. Attention is just a soft, learned lookup table.

glossary_data.tooltip: Q·Kᵀ — how well a query matches each key
Dividing by √dₖ keeps the scores from exploding
Scores become weights that blend the values V

title: Ideal Gas Law
author: Émile Clapeyron
description: Pressure, volume, moles, and temperature of a gas, all in one relation.
hook: A balloon shrinks in the freezer and swells in the sun. The ideal gas law ties pressure, volume, and temperature together so you can predict exactly how much.
hook_action: Drag temperature, volume, or the amount of gas and watch the balance shift.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the temperature T upward.
lessons_data.insight: At fixed volume, heating a gas raises its pressure — the molecules hit the walls harder and more often.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the volume V down to about 5 L.
lessons_data.insight: Squeeze the same gas into less space and the pressure climbs. Halve the volume, double the pressure — Boyle's law lives inside this equation.

lessons_data.instruction: Increase n, the amount of gas.
lessons_data.insight: More molecules in the same box means more collisions and higher pressure. R, the gas constant, is the fixed conversion that makes all of this line up.

glossary_data.tooltip: The universal gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K)

title: Arrhenius Equation
author: Svante Arrhenius
description: Why reactions speed up dramatically when you heat them.
hook: Milk lasts days in the fridge and hours on the counter. A 10°C rise can double a reaction rate. Arrhenius explains the exponential payoff of heat.
hook_action: Drag the temperature and the activation energy barrier.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the temperature T upward.
lessons_data.insight: Higher temperature means more molecules carry enough energy to clear the barrier, so the rate constant k climbs — fast.

lessons_data.instruction: Push T up to about 500 K.
lessons_data.insight: Because T sits inside an exponential, modest heating can multiply the rate many times over. This is why cooking and catalysis care so much about temperature.

lessons_data.instruction: Now raise the activation energy E_a toward 150.
lessons_data.insight: A taller barrier slows everything down exponentially. Catalysts work by lowering E_a, opening an easier path over the hill.

glossary_data.tooltip: T — raising it speeds the reaction
Eₐ — the energy hill reactants must clear
k — how fast the reaction proceeds

title: Henderson-Hasselbalch
author: Henderson, Hasselbalch
description: How a buffer holds its pH steady.
hook: Your blood stays at pH 7.4 even after a sour lemon or a hard workout. Buffers make that possible, and this equation is their control dial.
hook_action: Drag the ratio of base to acid and the acid's pKa.

variables_data.name: ratio
variables_data.description: Ratio of conjugate base to acid

lessons_data.instruction: Set the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] to 1.
lessons_data.insight: When base and acid are equal, log(1) = 0, so pH equals pKa exactly. This is the center of a buffer's working range.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the ratio up toward 10.
lessons_data.insight: Tenfold more base shifts pH up by exactly 1 unit. A buffer resists change best within about one pH unit of its pKa.

lessons_data.instruction: Change the pKa to pick a different acid.
lessons_data.insight: You choose a buffer by matching its pKa to the pH you want to hold. That is how chemists and your bloodstream lock in a target.

glossary_data.tooltip: pH at which half the acid is dissociated
[A⁻]/[HA] — the base-to-acid balance
Resists pH change near its pKa

title: Nernst Equation
author: Walther Nernst
description: The voltage of a battery as its chemistry runs down.
hook: A fresh battery reads 1.5 V; a dying one sags lower. The Nernst equation predicts the voltage from the concentrations inside the cell.
hook_action: Drag the standard potential, electrons transferred, and reaction quotient.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the reaction quotient Q to 1.
lessons_data.insight: At Q = 1, ln(1) = 0, so the cell sits exactly at its standard potential E⁰. This is the reference point for every electrochemical table.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag Q up toward 1000 (products piling up).
lessons_data.insight: As products accumulate, Q rises and the voltage drops. A battery is dead when Q reaches equilibrium and E falls to zero.

lessons_data.instruction: Change n, the number of electrons transferred.
lessons_data.insight: More electrons per reaction flattens the voltage's sensitivity to concentration. F, Faraday's constant, converts moles of electrons into charge.

glossary_data.tooltip: E⁰ — cell voltage at standard conditions
n — electrons transferred per reaction
Q — current ratio of products to reactants

title: Beer-Lambert Law
author: Beer, Lambert
description: How much light a solution absorbs tells you how concentrated it is.
hook: Deeper-colored juice is more concentrated — your eyes already do spectroscopy. Beer-Lambert turns that intuition into a precise measurement.
hook_action: Drag the concentration, path length, and how strongly the molecule absorbs.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the concentration c upward.
lessons_data.insight: Absorbance is directly proportional to concentration — twice the dye, twice the absorbance. This straight line is what makes the law so useful.

lessons_data.instruction: Now lengthen the path l toward 10 cm.
lessons_data.insight: Light passing through more solution meets more molecules, so absorbance scales with path length too. A longer cuvette boosts sensitivity.

lessons_data.instruction: Change ε, how strongly the molecule absorbs.
lessons_data.insight: ε is fixed by the molecule and the wavelength. Pick a wavelength where ε is large and even trace amounts become measurable — the heart of analytical chemistry.

glossary_data.tooltip: ε — how strongly the species absorbs light
l — distance light travels through the sample
c — amount of absorbing species present

title: Gibbs Free Energy
author: J. Willard Gibbs
description: Whether a reaction will happen on its own.
hook: Ice melts above 0°C and freezes below it — same process, opposite directions. Gibbs free energy says which way any reaction will spontaneously run.
hook_action: Drag enthalpy, entropy, and temperature to flip ΔG's sign.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the temperature T.
lessons_data.insight: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative when a reaction runs on its own. Temperature scales the entropy term, so it can flip the outcome.

lessons_data.instruction: Set ΔH positive (try the Endothermic preset).
lessons_data.insight: An energy-absorbing reaction looks unfavorable at first. But a large positive entropy plus enough heat can still make ΔG negative.

lessons_data.instruction: Now push the temperature up to about 900 K.
lessons_data.insight: At high temperature the −TΔS term dominates: entropy-driven reactions that refuse to go when cold suddenly become spontaneous. This is why heating drives so much chemistry.

glossary_data.tooltip: ΔH — heat released or absorbed
T — couples to the entropy term
ΔS — change in disorder
ΔG < 0 means the reaction proceeds on its own

title: Rate Law
author: Cato Guldberg, Peter Waage
description: How reaction speed depends on concentration.
hook: Why does a fire roar in pure oxygen but smolder in air? The rate law connects how fast a reaction goes to how much reactant is present — and the exponents are the surprise.
hook_action: Drag the concentration of A and the reaction order m.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the concentration [A] upward.
lessons_data.insight: For a first-order reaction, doubling [A] doubles the rate. The reaction speeds up as reactant piles up.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the order m to 2.
lessons_data.insight: A second-order reaction quadruples its rate when you double [A]. The exponent — which you can only find by experiment — controls how dramatically concentration matters.

lessons_data.instruction: Now set m to 0.
lessons_data.insight: A zero-order reaction ignores concentration entirely — its rate is just k. This happens when a surface or enzyme is saturated and working flat out.

glossary_data.tooltip: [A] — amount of reactant
m — how sensitively rate depends on [A]
k — the intrinsic speed of the reaction

title: Clausius-Clapeyron
author: Clausius, Clapeyron
description: Why water boils cooler on a mountain.
hook: On Everest, water boils at 71°C and you cannot brew a proper cup of tea. The Clausius-Clapeyron relation ties boiling point to pressure.
hook_action: Drag the temperature and the heat of vaporization.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the temperature T upward.
lessons_data.insight: The slope dP/dT tells you how steeply vapor pressure climbs with temperature. Near boiling, a small temperature change moves the pressure a lot.

lessons_data.instruction: Lower T toward 344 K (about 71°C).
lessons_data.insight: At reduced pressure, water reaches its boiling vapor pressure at a lower temperature — exactly the high-altitude tea problem.

lessons_data.instruction: Raise the heat of vaporization ΔH_vap.
lessons_data.insight: Liquids that take more energy to vaporize have steeper pressure-temperature curves. This single relation underlies pressure cookers, refrigerators, and weather.

glossary_data.tooltip: ΔH_vap — heat to turn liquid into gas
T — where the phase boundary sits
How vapour pressure climbs with temperature

title: Newton's Second Law
author: Isaac Newton
description: Force equals mass times acceleration — the engine of classical mechanics.
hook: Push a shopping cart and it rolls; push a loaded truck the same way and it barely budges. The same force produces different acceleration depending on mass.
hook_action: Drag the mass and the acceleration to feel how force responds.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the acceleration a upward.
lessons_data.insight: Force is proportional to acceleration. To speed up faster, you need more force — every time.

lessons_data.instruction: Now increase the mass m.
lessons_data.insight: Heavier objects need more force for the same acceleration. Mass is exactly the resistance to being accelerated — inertia made quantitative.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the mass near its maximum.
lessons_data.insight: A huge mass barely accelerates under a modest force. This is why rockets need enormous thrust and why stopping a train takes kilometers.

glossary_data.tooltip: m — resistance to being accelerated
a — the rate of change of velocity
F = ma — the push that results

title: Kinetic Energy
author: Gottfried Leibniz
description: The energy of motion grows with the square of speed.
hook: A car at 60 mph has four times the crash energy of one at 30 mph — not twice. That squared term is why speed limits matter so much.
hook_action: Drag the speed and watch energy climb far faster than the speed itself.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the speed v upward.
lessons_data.insight: Energy depends on v², so doubling the speed quadruples the energy. Speed matters far more than mass here.

lessons_data.instruction: Push v to about 20 (then imagine doubling it).
lessons_data.insight: Going from 10 to 20 m/s is a 4× jump in energy. That extra energy must go somewhere in a crash — into crumpling metal.

lessons_data.instruction: Now change the mass m.
lessons_data.insight: Mass matters linearly — double the mass, double the energy — but speed matters quadratically. That asymmetry shapes everything from car safety to ballistics.

glossary_data.tooltip: m — heavier means more energy
v — energy grows with its square
½mv² — the energy of motion

title: Coulomb's Law
author: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb
description: The electric force between charges, an inverse-square twin of gravity.
hook: Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall. Coulomb's law is the force doing the sticking — and it falls off with distance just like gravity.
hook_action: Drag the charges and the distance between them.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the separation r and watch the force change.
lessons_data.insight: Force falls off with the square of distance — move twice as far and the force drops to a quarter.

lessons_data.instruction: Bring r down toward 0.1.
lessons_data.insight: Up close the force becomes enormous. The r² in the denominator is what makes nearby charges grip so hard.

lessons_data.instruction: Make one charge negative.
lessons_data.insight: Same signs repel, opposite signs attract. Unlike gravity, the electric force comes in two flavors — which is why atoms can both bind and push apart.

glossary_data.tooltip: q — like charges repel, opposite attract
r — force falls off as 1/r²
The electrostatic push between charges

title: Ohm's Law
author: Georg Ohm
description: Voltage, current, and resistance in the simplest circuit relation.
hook: Why does a thin wire get hot and a thick one stay cool? Ohm's law links the push (voltage), the flow (current), and the friction (resistance).
hook_action: Drag the current and the resistance to see the voltage respond.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the resistance R upward.
lessons_data.insight: At a fixed current, more resistance needs more voltage to push the charge through.

lessons_data.instruction: Now increase the current I.
lessons_data.insight: Voltage rises with current too. The three quantities lock together: fix any two and the third is determined.

lessons_data.instruction: Set R very low while I is high.
lessons_data.insight: Low resistance and high current means power (I²R) dumps as heat — exactly what happens in a short circuit, and why fuses exist.

glossary_data.tooltip: I — the flow of charge
R — opposition to the current
V = IR — the driving push

title: Snell's Law
author: Willebrord Snellius
description: How light bends when it crosses between materials.
hook: A straw in a glass of water looks broken at the surface. Light bends as it slows down entering the water — and Snell's law says by exactly how much.
hook_action: Drag the incidence angle and the refractive indices.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the angle of incidence θ₁.
lessons_data.insight: Light entering a denser medium bends toward the normal. The steeper the entry, the more dramatic the bend.

lessons_data.instruction: Raise n₂, the index of the second medium.
lessons_data.insight: A higher index means light slows more and bends more sharply. This is exactly how a lens focuses light to a point.

lessons_data.instruction: Set θ₁ near 80° going into a denser medium.
lessons_data.insight: Reverse the direction and at steep angles light can't escape at all — total internal reflection. That trapped light is what carries the internet through fiber optics.

glossary_data.tooltip: θ — measured from the surface normal
n — how much a medium slows light
Light bends toward the slower medium

title: Doppler Effect
author: Christian Doppler
description: Why a passing siren drops in pitch.
hook: An ambulance races toward you — high pitch — then past you — low pitch. The sound waves bunch up ahead and stretch out behind. Same trick reveals the expanding universe.
hook_action: Drag the source speed and watch the heard frequency shift.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the source speed positive (toward you).
lessons_data.insight: As the source approaches, each wave is emitted a little closer than the last, so the waves bunch up and the pitch rises.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the source speed negative.
lessons_data.insight: Moving away stretches the waves and the pitch drops. That sudden high-to-low flip as the ambulance passes is the Doppler effect you hear.

lessons_data.instruction: Change the source frequency f.
lessons_data.insight: The shift is proportional to the original frequency. Astronomers use the same idea on light: galaxies are redshifted because the universe is stretching them away.

glossary_data.tooltip: f — the perceived pitch of the wave
v_s — speed of the emitter
Approaching raises pitch, receding lowers it

title: Stefan-Boltzmann Law
author: Stefan, Boltzmann
description: How brightly a hot object glows — with a ferocious fourth power.
hook: An electric stove glows dull red; the Sun blazes white. A modest rise in temperature makes a huge jump in radiated power, because of that T⁴.
hook_action: Drag the temperature and watch radiated power explode.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the temperature T upward.
lessons_data.insight: Radiated power scales with T to the fourth power. Double the temperature and you radiate sixteen times as much energy.

lessons_data.instruction: Push T up toward 5800 K (the Sun's surface).
lessons_data.insight: That brutal fourth power is why stars are so luminous and why a small temperature error in climate models matters so much.

lessons_data.instruction: Change the surface area A.
lessons_data.insight: Power scales linearly with area but with the fourth power of temperature. Temperature, not size, dominates how bright something glows.

glossary_data.tooltip: T — radiated power scales as T⁴
A — a larger surface radiates more
Total energy a hot body emits

title: de Broglie Wavelength
author: Louis de Broglie
description: Every moving particle is also a wave.
hook: Electrons make interference patterns just like light. de Broglie said all matter has a wavelength — we just never notice it for anything bigger than an atom.
hook_action: Drag the mass and speed to see the wavelength shrink toward nothing.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the speed v upward.
lessons_data.insight: Faster particles have shorter wavelengths. This is why electron microscopes accelerate electrons hard — to get a tiny wavelength and sharp images.

lessons_data.instruction: Now increase the mass toward a proton (1836).
lessons_data.insight: Heavier particles have far shorter wavelengths. A baseball's wavelength is so absurdly small we can never observe its wave nature.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the speed back down low.
lessons_data.insight: Slow, light particles have the longest, most observable wavelengths. This wave-particle duality is the strange heart of quantum mechanics.

glossary_data.tooltip: m — heavier means a shorter wavelength
v — faster means a shorter wavelength
λ = h/mv — matter behaving as a wave

title: Heisenberg Uncertainty
author: Werner Heisenberg
description: You cannot know both position and momentum perfectly.
hook: Pin down exactly where a particle is, and its speed becomes a total blur. This isn't a measurement flaw — it's a hard limit baked into reality.
hook_action: Squeeze the position uncertainty and watch momentum uncertainty blow up.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the position uncertainty Δx upward.
lessons_data.insight: A larger Δx means you know the position only roughly — which lets the momentum be sharply defined.

lessons_data.instruction: Now squeeze Δx down toward 0.01.
lessons_data.insight: The tighter you locate the particle, the more its momentum must spread out, because their product can't drop below ℏ/2.

lessons_data.instruction: Set Δx to atomic scale (~0.1 nm).
lessons_data.insight: Confine an electron to an atom and its momentum uncertainty is enormous — that restless motion is exactly why electrons don't fall into the nucleus.

glossary_data.tooltip: Δx — uncertainty in location
Δp — pinning one blurs the other
Their product can't drop below ℏ/2

title: Planck's Relation
author: Max Planck
description: Light comes in packets of energy set by its frequency.
hook: Why does UV light burn your skin but red light doesn't? Because energy comes in chunks proportional to frequency — and only high-frequency chunks pack enough punch.
hook_action: Drag the frequency and watch each photon's energy rise.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the frequency ν upward.
lessons_data.insight: Energy is exactly proportional to frequency. Bluer light carries more energy per photon than redder light.

lessons_data.instruction: Push ν up into the ultraviolet (~15).
lessons_data.insight: Above a threshold, each photon finally carries enough energy to knock electrons loose or damage DNA. This quantized jump is the photoelectric effect — Einstein's Nobel work.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag ν back down to red light.
lessons_data.insight: No matter how bright you make red light, each photon is too weak to do UV's job. Energy depends on frequency, not brightness — the insight that launched quantum theory.

glossary_data.tooltip: ν — the colour of the light
Energy arrives in discrete packets
E = hν — the energy of one photon

title: Lorentz Force
author: Hendrik Lorentz
description: The force on a charge moving through electric and magnetic fields.
hook: A magnet bends a beam of electrons in an old TV; the same force spins every electric motor and paints the northern lights across the sky.
hook_action: Drag the charge's speed and the magnetic field strength.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the speed v upward.
lessons_data.insight: The magnetic part of the force only acts on moving charges — and grows with speed. A stationary charge feels nothing from the magnetic field.

lessons_data.instruction: Now raise the magnetic field B.
lessons_data.insight: A stronger field curves the charge more tightly. Cyclotrons and mass spectrometers use exactly this to bend particles into circles.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the speed v to zero.
lessons_data.insight: With v = 0 the magnetic force vanishes and only the electric field pushes. The v×B cross product is why magnetism is really electricity seen from a moving frame.

glossary_data.tooltip: q — the moving particle's charge
v — only moving charges feel the magnetic part
B — bends the path perpendicular to motion

title: Hardy-Weinberg Principle
author: Hardy, Weinberg
description: How allele frequencies stay constant in an idealized population.
hook: If brown eyes are dominant, why don't they take over and eliminate blue eyes? Hardy-Weinberg shows that, left alone, gene frequencies don't drift — they hold steady.
hook_action: Drag the allele frequency p and watch the genotype mix.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the allele frequency p.
lessons_data.insight: p is the fraction of one allele; q = 1 − p is the other. The three genotype frequencies (p², 2pq, q²) always sum to 1.

lessons_data.instruction: Set p to about 0.5.
lessons_data.insight: Heterozygous carriers (2pq) peak when the alleles are balanced — half the population at p = 0.5. This is why recessive traits hide in carriers.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag p down toward 0.1.
lessons_data.insight: When an allele is rare, almost every copy hides in a carrier rather than showing up as the recessive trait. That's why rare genetic diseases persist quietly for generations.

glossary_data.tooltip: p — fraction of one allele in the pool
p², 2pq, q² — the expected genotype shares
Frequencies stay fixed without selection

title: Logistic Growth
author: Pierre Verhulst
description: Populations grow fast, then level off at the limit of their resources.
hook: Bacteria in a dish double and double — then suddenly stop. No environment has infinite food. Logistic growth is the S-curve every real population follows.
hook_action: Drag the population, growth rate, and carrying capacity.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the population N upward toward K.
lessons_data.insight: Growth is fastest when N is small and there's room to spare. As N approaches the carrying capacity K, the (1 − N/K) brake kicks in.

lessons_data.instruction: Set N very close to K.
lessons_data.insight: Near capacity, growth nearly stops — the resources are used up. This is the flat top of the S-curve where the population plateaus.

lessons_data.instruction: Change the growth rate r.
lessons_data.insight: r sets how quickly the population climbs the curve. Push r too high in the discrete version of this equation and you get chaos — the same logistic map behind chaos theory.

glossary_data.tooltip: N — the current number of individuals
r — the intrinsic reproduction rate
K — the ceiling the environment allows

title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
author: Michaelis, Menten
description: How fast an enzyme works as substrate piles up.
hook: An enzyme speeds up as you feed it more substrate — but only to a point. Once every enzyme is busy, adding more does nothing. This curve describes nearly all enzymes.
hook_action: Drag the substrate concentration and the enzyme's parameters.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the substrate concentration [S] upward.
lessons_data.insight: At low substrate the rate climbs almost linearly — the enzyme has plenty of free capacity.

lessons_data.instruction: Push [S] up high.
lessons_data.insight: Eventually every enzyme is occupied and the rate flattens at Vmax. More substrate can't help when there are no free enzymes left.

lessons_data.instruction: Lower the Michaelis constant K_m.
lessons_data.insight: K_m is the substrate level for half-maximum speed — a measure of affinity. A small K_m means the enzyme grabs substrate eagerly and saturates early.

glossary_data.tooltip: [S] — concentration feeding the enzyme
K_m — the [S] giving half the maximum rate
V_max — speed when the enzyme is saturated

title: DNA Base Pairing
author: Watson, Crick
description: The complementary rule that lets DNA copy itself.
hook: A always pairs with T, G always with C. That rigid rule is why one strand of DNA contains all the information to rebuild the other — the basis of all inheritance.
hook_action: Drag the GC content and watch how tightly the helix holds together.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the GC content upward.
lessons_data.insight: G-C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds; A-T pairs by only two. More G-C means a more tightly bound double helix.

lessons_data.instruction: Push GC content up toward 80%.
lessons_data.insight: GC-rich DNA needs more heat to separate the strands — a higher melting temperature. Organisms in hot springs tend to have GC-rich genomes for exactly this reason.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag GC content down low.
lessons_data.insight: AT-rich regions unzip easily — which is why replication and transcription often start there. The pairing rule turns sequence into mechanical behavior.

glossary_data.tooltip: Fraction of G–C base pairs
G–C share three hydrogen bonds, A–T only two
More G–C makes a hotter-melting, stabler helix

title: Goldman Equation
author: Goldman, Hodgkin, Katz
description: The voltage across a living cell's membrane.
hook: Every neuron in your brain holds a tiny voltage across its membrane, set by ion concentrations. Flip that voltage and a thought fires. The Goldman equation gives its resting value.
hook_action: Drag the outside potassium and sodium concentrations.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the outside potassium concentration upward.
lessons_data.insight: The membrane is far more permeable to potassium, so external K⁺ dominates the resting voltage. Raise it and the cell depolarizes.

lessons_data.instruction: Push outside potassium up toward 15 mM.
lessons_data.insight: High external potassium pulls the membrane voltage toward zero — which is why potassium imbalances can stop the heart. Tiny ion changes carry life-or-death stakes.

lessons_data.instruction: Now change the outside sodium.
lessons_data.insight: Sodium has only a small effect at rest because the membrane barely lets it through. But open sodium channels and that stored gradient drives the spike of a nerve impulse.

glossary_data.tooltip: [K⁺] — the dominant ion at rest
[Na⁺] — drives the depolarising swing
Resting voltage across the membrane

title: Lotka-Volterra Equations
author: Lotka, Volterra
description: The boom-and-bust cycle of predators and prey.
hook: Lots of rabbits, foxes feast and multiply; too many foxes, rabbits crash, then foxes starve. Predator and prey populations chase each other in endless cycles.
hook_action: Drag the prey growth rate and the predation rate.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the prey growth rate α upward.
lessons_data.insight: With few predators, prey multiply almost exponentially — the αx term. This is the boom half of the cycle.

lessons_data.instruction: Now raise the predation rate β.
lessons_data.insight: The βxy term is where predators eat prey — it grows when both are abundant. Crank it up and the prey population gets driven down hard.

lessons_data.instruction: Set β high while α stays moderate.
lessons_data.insight: Strong predation crashes the prey, then the predators starve, then prey recover — the famous out-of-phase cycle seen in real lynx and hare records.

glossary_data.tooltip: x — the prey population
β — rate at which predators consume prey
Predator and prey rise and fall out of phase

title: Compound Interest
author: Jacob Bernoulli
description: Money that earns money on money — exponential growth.
hook: Save $1,000 at 7% and in 40 years it's nearly $15,000 — you barely lifted a finger. Compound interest is the closest thing to magic in personal finance.
hook_action: Drag the rate and the number of years and watch the balance snowball.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the number of years t upward.
lessons_data.insight: Because t is in the exponent, balance grows faster and faster over time. The longest stretch of years does the heaviest lifting.

lessons_data.instruction: Push t out to 40 years.
lessons_data.insight: Most of the growth happens in the final years — the curve bends sharply upward. Starting early beats saving more later.

lessons_data.instruction: Now change the interest rate r.
lessons_data.insight: Even a couple of extra percentage points compounds into a huge difference over decades. This is why fees and returns matter enormously over a lifetime.

glossary_data.tooltip: P — the starting amount
r — the interest rate per period
Interest earns interest over time

title: Supply and Demand
author: Alfred Marshall
description: Where buyers and sellers meet sets the price.
hook: Raise the price and shoppers buy less while producers make more. The price where those two forces balance is the market price — no committee required.
hook_action: Drag the price and watch quantity demanded and supplied diverge.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the price P upward.
lessons_data.insight: As price rises, quantity demanded falls (a − bP) while quantity supplied rises (c + dP). Buyers and sellers pull in opposite directions.

lessons_data.instruction: Push the price up high.
lessons_data.insight: At a high price, supply outruns demand — a surplus of unsold goods. That glut pressures sellers to cut prices back down.

lessons_data.instruction: Now bring the price to around 50.
lessons_data.insight: At equilibrium, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied — the market clears with no shortage or surplus. This self-correcting balance is the heart of free markets.

glossary_data.tooltip: P — adjusts until the market clears
Where quantity supplied meets quantity demanded
A mispriced market over- or under-supplies

title: GDP Expenditure
author: Simon Kuznets
description: A nation's output, added up from how it's spent.
hook: When politicians argue about "the economy", this is the number. GDP sums everything a country produces — by adding up consumption, investment, government, and net trade.
hook_action: Drag the spending components and watch total output respond.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag consumption C upward.
lessons_data.insight: Consumer spending is usually the biggest slice of GDP — often around two-thirds. When shoppers stop spending, output sags.

lessons_data.instruction: Raise government spending G toward 40.
lessons_data.insight: In a downturn, governments boost G to make up for falling C and I. That's the logic behind stimulus packages and public works programs.

lessons_data.instruction: Change investment I.
lessons_data.insight: Investment — factories, housing, equipment — is the most volatile component, swinging hard between booms and busts. The (X − M) trade term can be positive or negative.

glossary_data.tooltip: C — household spending
I — business spending on capital
G — public spending

title: Fisher Equation
author: Irving Fisher
description: How inflation eats into the interest you actually earn.
hook: Your savings account pays 3%, but prices rose 4% — you actually lost money. The Fisher equation separates the headline rate from your real return.
hook_action: Drag the real rate and inflation to see the nominal rate change.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the inflation rate π upward.
lessons_data.insight: To keep the same real return, the nominal rate i must rise with inflation. Lenders demand it; this is why rates climb when prices do.

lessons_data.instruction: Push inflation up toward 12%.
lessons_data.insight: When inflation spikes, nominal rates have to chase it just to break even. Borrowers love high inflation; savers in cash get quietly robbed.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the real rate r negative.
lessons_data.insight: A negative real rate means your money loses purchasing power even while it earns interest. Central banks sometimes engineer this on purpose to push people to spend.

glossary_data.tooltip: The stated, before-inflation interest rate
π — erodes purchasing power
Nominal rate minus inflation

title: Capital Asset Pricing Model
author: William Sharpe
description: The return you should expect for taking on market risk.
hook: Why should a volatile tech stock pay more than a government bond? CAPM says: only the risk you can't diversify away earns extra return — and beta measures it.
hook_action: Drag beta and the market return to price the risk.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag beta β upward.
lessons_data.insight: Beta measures how much a stock swings with the market. Higher beta means more risk — and CAPM says investors demand more expected return to bear it.

lessons_data.instruction: Set beta to 0.
lessons_data.insight: A beta of zero means no market risk, so the expected return collapses to the risk-free rate. That's the return on a government bond — the floor for everything else.

lessons_data.instruction: Push beta up to 2.
lessons_data.insight: A beta of 2 amplifies the market's risk premium twofold — bigger gains in booms, bigger losses in busts. CAPM turns that risk into a precise required return.

glossary_data.tooltip: β — how much an asset swings with the market
R_f — the return that carries no risk
R_m — return of the whole market

title: Nash Equilibrium
author: John Nash
description: A stable outcome where no one can gain by changing alone.
hook: Two suspects are interrogated separately. Each is better off betraying the other — so both confess, even though staying silent would help them both. Welcome to the prisoner's dilemma.
hook_action: Drag the temptation to defect and watch cooperation collapse.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the temptation to defect T upward.
lessons_data.insight: As betraying becomes more rewarding, cooperation gets harder to sustain. Each player reasons the same way, independently.

lessons_data.instruction: Push T up into prisoner's-dilemma territory.
lessons_data.insight: When defecting always beats cooperating no matter what the other does, both defect — even though mutual cooperation would have been better. That mutual betrayal is the Nash equilibrium.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag T back down low.
lessons_data.insight: With little temptation, cooperation becomes the stable equilibrium. Repeated games, reputations, and contracts all work by lowering the payoff to defection.

glossary_data.tooltip: A plan no player wants to change alone
The reward each outcome pays out
Stable when unilateral defection doesn't help

title: Cobb-Douglas Production
author: Cobb, Douglas
description: How capital and labor combine to produce output.
hook: A factory needs both machines and workers. Add more of either and output grows — but each new machine, with workers fixed, helps a little less. Diminishing returns, quantified.
hook_action: Drag capital, labor, and the capital share α.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag capital K upward.
lessons_data.insight: Adding capital raises output — but because the exponent α is less than 1, each extra unit adds a little less. That's diminishing returns.

lessons_data.instruction: Now increase labor L.
lessons_data.insight: Labor and capital both contribute, weighted by α and (1 − α). Output grows fastest when you scale both together rather than piling on just one.

lessons_data.instruction: Change the capital share α.
lessons_data.insight: α sets how much capital versus labor drives output. Economists estimate it around 0.3 for whole economies — labor earns roughly two-thirds of the pie.

glossary_data.tooltip: K — machines and tools
L — the workforce
Production from combining capital and labour

title: Standard Deviation
author: Karl Pearson
description: A single number for how spread out data is.
hook: Two classes both average 75 on a test. In one, everyone scored near 75; in the other, scores ranged from 40 to 100. The average hides that — standard deviation reveals it.
hook_action: Drag the spread and watch the data tighten or scatter.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the spread σ upward.
lessons_data.insight: Standard deviation measures the typical distance of a data point from the mean. A bigger σ means the data is more scattered.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the spread down low.
lessons_data.insight: A small σ means values cluster tightly around the average — predictable, consistent data. Manufacturing quality control lives and dies by keeping σ small.

lessons_data.instruction: Now push the spread up high.
lessons_data.insight: A large σ means the average tells you little about any single point. About 68% of normal data falls within one σ of the mean — the rule that turns σ into probability.

glossary_data.tooltip: σ — the typical distance from the mean
σ² — the average squared deviation
The centre the spread is measured from

title: Linear Regression
author: Francis Galton
description: Drawing the best straight line through a cloud of points.
hook: Does studying more raise your grade? Plot the data and fit a line. Its slope tells you how much, on average, one variable moves with another — the workhorse of data science.
hook_action: Drag the slope and intercept to fit the trend.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the slope β₁.
lessons_data.insight: The slope is the heart of the model: how much y changes for each one-unit step in x. A positive slope rises, a negative one falls.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the slope to 0.
lessons_data.insight: A zero slope means x tells you nothing about y — no relationship. Detecting whether the true slope is really nonzero is the point of a significance test.

lessons_data.instruction: Now change the intercept β₀.
lessons_data.insight: The intercept shifts the whole line up or down — the predicted y when x is zero. Regression finds the β₀ and β₁ that minimize the total squared error ε.

glossary_data.tooltip: β₁ — change in y per unit of x
β₀ — the value of y when x is zero
The line minimising squared residuals

title: Chi-Square Test
author: Karl Pearson
description: Does the data match what you expected, or not?
hook: You flip a coin 100 times and get 60 heads. Is it rigged, or just luck? Chi-square measures how far observed counts stray from expected — and whether that gap is suspicious.
hook_action: Drag the observed count away from the expected and watch χ² climb.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the observed count equal to the expected.
lessons_data.insight: When observed equals expected, the gap is zero and so is χ². The data perfectly matches the hypothesis.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the observed count up toward 90.
lessons_data.insight: The bigger the gap between observed and expected, the larger χ² grows — and squaring makes big deviations count far more than small ones.

lessons_data.instruction: Change the expected count E.
lessons_data.insight: Dividing by E means the same absolute gap matters more when few events were expected. Cross a χ² threshold and you reject the hypothesis as too unlikely to be chance.

glossary_data.tooltip: O — the counts you actually measured
E — the counts the null hypothesis predicts
How far observed strays from expected

title: Central Limit Theorem
author: Laplace, Lyapunov
description: Why averages are always bell-shaped, whatever the data.
hook: Roll one die and the outcomes are flat. Average ten dice and you get a bell curve. The central limit theorem is why the normal distribution shows up absolutely everywhere.
hook_action: Drag the sample size and watch the distribution of the average narrow.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the sample size n upward.
lessons_data.insight: The distribution of the sample mean has variance σ²/n — so as n grows, the average becomes more tightly pinned around the true mean.

lessons_data.instruction: Set n to about 30.
lessons_data.insight: By around n = 30, the sampling distribution looks reliably bell-shaped even if the raw data was skewed. That's the rule of thumb behind countless statistical tests.

lessons_data.instruction: Push n up to its maximum.
lessons_data.insight: Quadruple the sample size and you only halve the error — precision improves with √n, not n. This is why big studies are expensive: certainty gets pricey fast.

glossary_data.tooltip: n — observations averaged together
Sample means approach a bell curve
The spread of the mean shrinks as 1/√n

title: Poisson Distribution
author: Siméon Poisson
description: The math of rare, random events over time.
hook: How many buses arrive in an hour? How many typos on a page? For rare independent events with a steady average rate, the Poisson distribution predicts the spread.
hook_action: Drag the average rate λ and the count k.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the average rate λ upward.
lessons_data.insight: λ is the mean number of events per interval. As it rises, the most likely count rises with it — and the whole distribution shifts right.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the count k to match λ.
lessons_data.insight: The probability peaks when k is near λ. Asking for a count far from the average — many events when few are expected — becomes vanishingly unlikely.

lessons_data.instruction: Set λ low (around 1) and k high.
lessons_data.insight: A high count when the rate is low is extremely improbable — exactly how Poisson flags surprising clusters, from disease outbreaks to server failures.

glossary_data.tooltip: λ — the average number of events per interval
k — how many actually occur
Models independent, rare events

title: Markov Chain
author: Andrey Markov
description: The future depends only on the present, not the past.
hook: Predict tomorrow's weather from today's, ignoring last week entirely. This "memoryless" assumption powers Google's PageRank, text generators, and board-game odds alike.
hook_action: Drag the transition probability and watch the system's behavior shift.

variables_data.name: p
variables_data.description: Probability of staying in the same state

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the transition probability p.
lessons_data.insight: p is the chance the system stays put each step. The next state depends only on the current one — never on how you got there.

lessons_data.instruction: Push p up toward 0.9.
lessons_data.insight: A high stay-probability makes states sticky — sunny days tend to follow sunny days. The chain lingers, and long runs of the same state become common.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag p down toward 0.1.
lessons_data.insight: A low stay-probability makes the system flip constantly. Over many steps a Markov chain settles into a steady-state distribution — the math behind PageRank ranking the whole web.

glossary_data.tooltip: p — probability of switching state
Where the system currently sits
The next step depends only on the present

title: Hooke's Law
author: Robert Hooke
description: A spring pushes back in proportion to how far you stretch it.
hook: Stretch a spring twice as far and it pulls back twice as hard. This simple linear law sits inside every scale, mattress, and car suspension.
hook_action: Drag the displacement and the spring stiffness.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the displacement x.
lessons_data.insight: The restoring force grows in direct proportion to displacement — and the minus sign means it always points back toward rest.

lessons_data.instruction: Now raise the spring constant k.
lessons_data.insight: A stiffer spring (larger k) fights back harder for the same stretch. k is exactly the slope of the force-versus-stretch line.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag x negative to compress the spring.
lessons_data.insight: Compress instead of stretch and the force flips direction — still pushing back toward rest. This restoring force is what makes springs oscillate and clocks tick.

glossary_data.tooltip: k — how stiff the spring is
x — distance from the rest position
Pulls the spring back toward rest

title: Stress and Strain
author: Thomas Young
description: How stiff a material is, captured in one number.
hook: Pull on a rubber band and it stretches a lot; pull on a steel cable and it barely moves. Young's modulus E is the number that says how stiff a material is.
hook_action: Drag the strain and the material's stiffness E.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the strain ε upward.
lessons_data.insight: Strain is the fractional stretch. For a given material, stress rises in step with strain — the steeper the line, the stiffer the material.

lessons_data.instruction: Set E high (toward steel or diamond).
lessons_data.insight: A large Young's modulus means huge stress for even a tiny stretch. This is why steel beams barely flex under enormous loads.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag E way down (rubber).
lessons_data.insight: A low modulus stretches easily under little stress. Engineers pick materials by matching this stiffness to the job — rigid where it must hold, flexible where it must bend.

glossary_data.tooltip: E — the material's stiffness
ε — the fractional deformation
Internal force per unit area

title: Bernoulli's Equation
author: Daniel Bernoulli
description: Faster-moving fluid has lower pressure.
hook: Why does an airplane wing lift? Air rushes faster over the curved top, dropping the pressure there. Bernoulli's equation trades fluid speed for pressure.
hook_action: Drag the flow speed and the height.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the flow speed v upward.
lessons_data.insight: Since the total stays constant, speeding the fluid up forces the pressure term down. Fast flow means low pressure.

lessons_data.instruction: Push v up high (a narrow, fast section).
lessons_data.insight: Where a pipe narrows, the fluid speeds up and its pressure plummets. This is the Venturi effect — and the suction that pulls fuel into an old carburetor.

lessons_data.instruction: Now raise the height h.
lessons_data.insight: Lifting the fluid spends energy on the ρgh term, leaving less for pressure and motion. Speed, height, and pressure all trade against one fixed total.

glossary_data.tooltip: v — faster flow means lower pressure
h — elevation within the flow
Trades off against speed and height

title: Transfer Function
author: Oliver Heaviside
description: How a system turns an input signal into an output.
hook: A cruise control, a thermostat, a guitar amp — each takes an input and produces an output. The transfer function is the compact recipe for that relationship.
hook_action: Drag the system gain and how fast it responds.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the gain K upward.
lessons_data.insight: Gain sets how strongly the output responds to the input — a small change in can become a big change out.

lessons_data.instruction: Now change the pole p.
lessons_data.insight: The pole controls how fast the system reacts. A large pole snaps to the new value quickly; a small one drifts there slowly.

lessons_data.instruction: Push the gain K high.
lessons_data.insight: Too much gain can make a feedback system overshoot and ring — or even go unstable. Tuning the transfer function is the central craft of control engineering.

glossary_data.tooltip: K — the overall amplification
p — where the response blows up
Poles in the left half-plane stay stable

title: Nyquist Stability Criterion
author: Harry Nyquist
description: Will a feedback loop stay stable or spiral out of control?
hook: Point a microphone at its own speaker and you get a screaming feedback howl. Every control loop risks the same runaway. Nyquist's count tells you whether yours is safe.
hook_action: Drag the encirclements and unstable open-loop poles.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the number of encirclements N.
lessons_data.insight: N counts how many times the system's frequency response loops around the critical −1 point. Z = N + P is the number of unstable closed-loop poles.

lessons_data.instruction: Set both N and P to 0.
lessons_data.insight: No encirclements and no unstable open-loop poles means Z = 0 — the closed loop is stable. This is the configuration every controller aims for.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drive N up to 2 with P at 0.
lessons_data.insight: Encircling −1 with no unstable poles to cancel means Z is positive — the loop will oscillate and blow up. That's the mathematical signature of the feedback howl.

glossary_data.tooltip: P — unstable open-loop poles
N — times the plot circles the −1 point
Z = N + P must be zero for stability

title: Reynolds Number
author: Osborne Reynolds
description: Smooth flow or chaotic turbulence? One number decides.
hook: Water from a tap can run glass-smooth or break into churning chaos. The Reynolds number predicts the switch — and lets engineers test a ship design in a small tank.
hook_action: Drag the speed, size, and viscosity to cross into turbulence.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the flow velocity v upward.
lessons_data.insight: Faster flow raises the Reynolds number. Below about 2000 the flow is smooth and layered; above about 4000 it tumbles into turbulence.

lessons_data.instruction: Push velocity and length up while viscosity is low.
lessons_data.insight: High speed, large size, and thin fluid all push Re sky-high and the flow becomes turbulent — the chaotic regime that makes the Navier-Stokes equations so hard.

lessons_data.instruction: Now raise the viscosity µ.
lessons_data.insight: Thick, sticky fluids resist turbulence and keep flow laminar even when fast. Because Re is dimensionless, a tiny model in a tank can faithfully mimic a full-size ship.

glossary_data.tooltip: v — the flow speed
L — the characteristic size
µ — the fluid's resistance to flow
A high Reynolds number means chaotic flow

title: Kepler's Third Law
author: Johannes Kepler
description: How long a planet takes to orbit depends on its distance.
hook: Mercury whips around the Sun in 88 days; Neptune takes 165 years. The further out a planet sits, the dramatically slower it orbits — and Kepler nailed the exact rule.
hook_action: Drag the orbit size and the central mass.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the orbit size a outward.
lessons_data.insight: Orbital period grows with a to the 3/2 power. Double the distance and the year gets nearly three times longer.

lessons_data.instruction: Push a out toward Neptune's orbit (~30 AU).
lessons_data.insight: Distant planets crawl around enormous orbits — Neptune's year is 165 of ours. The a³ in the law makes outer orbits brutally slow.

lessons_data.instruction: Now change the central mass M.
lessons_data.insight: A heavier star pulls harder, speeding orbits up. Astronomers run this backward: time an orbit, and the law weighs the star or hidden black hole at its center.

glossary_data.tooltip: a — the size of the orbit
M — the mass of the central body
T — how long one orbit takes

title: Hubble's Law
author: Edwin Hubble
description: Distant galaxies fly away faster — the universe is expanding.
hook: Every galaxy is rushing away from us, and the farther one is, the faster it flees. This isn't us being unpopular — space itself is stretching.
hook_action: Drag a galaxy's distance and watch its recession speed climb.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the galaxy's distance d outward.
lessons_data.insight: Recession speed is simply distance times the Hubble constant. Twice as far means twice as fast — a clean straight line across the cosmos.

lessons_data.instruction: Push d out toward 1000 Mpc.
lessons_data.insight: The most distant galaxies recede at a sizeable fraction of light speed. Far enough out, they slip beyond our horizon — their light can never reach us.

lessons_data.instruction: Now change the Hubble constant H₀.
lessons_data.insight: H₀ is the expansion rate, and its inverse estimates the age of the universe. Pinning down its exact value is one of cosmology's hottest open arguments.

glossary_data.tooltip: d — how far the galaxy is
H₀ — the expansion rate of the universe
More distant galaxies recede faster

title: Schwarzschild Radius
author: Karl Schwarzschild
description: Squeeze any mass small enough and it becomes a black hole.
hook: Crush the Earth to the size of a marble and not even light could escape it. The Schwarzschild radius is the point of no return for any given mass.
hook_action: Drag the mass and watch the event horizon grow.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the mass M upward.
lessons_data.insight: The event horizon radius is directly proportional to mass. Pile on more mass and the point of no return expands outward.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the mass to 1 solar mass.
lessons_data.insight: Compress the entire Sun inside a radius of just 3 km and it would become a black hole. Our Sun is nowhere near dense enough — it never will.

lessons_data.instruction: Push the mass up to a million suns.
lessons_data.insight: Supermassive black holes lurk at galaxy centers, with horizons larger than our Solar System. The one in M87 was the first ever photographed.

glossary_data.tooltip: M — the collapsed mass of the black hole
The radius of no return
Below it, not even light escapes

title: Stellar Luminosity
author: Stefan, Boltzmann
description: A star's total power, from its size and temperature.
hook: A small white-hot star can outshine a huge cool red one. A star's brightness depends on its surface area and, ferociously, on the fourth power of its temperature.
hook_action: Drag the radius and surface temperature.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the surface temperature T upward.
lessons_data.insight: Luminosity scales with T to the fourth power. A modest temperature rise makes a star vastly brighter — temperature dominates.

lessons_data.instruction: Push T up toward a blue giant (~30000 K).
lessons_data.insight: Hot blue stars blaze with enormous luminosity and burn through their fuel fast — living only millions of years instead of billions.

lessons_data.instruction: Now expand the radius R.
lessons_data.insight: A bloated red giant is cool yet luminous simply because it's so vast. Plotting luminosity against temperature for many stars gives the famous Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.

glossary_data.tooltip: R — the size of the star
T — surface temperature, raised to the 4th power
The total power the star radiates

title: Drake Equation
author: Frank Drake
description: An estimate for how many alien civilizations we might hear.
hook: Are we alone? The Drake equation doesn't answer that — it organizes our ignorance into factors, then shows how wildly the estimate swings on a few guesses.
hook_action: Drag the most uncertain factors and watch N explode or collapse.

variables_data.name: fl
variables_data.description: Fraction of worlds that develop life

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the civilization lifetime L upward.
lessons_data.insight: L — how long a civilization broadcasts — multiplies the whole result. The longer civilizations last, the more of them exist at once to detect.

lessons_data.instruction: Push every factor high (try the Optimistic preset).
lessons_data.insight: Generous guesses give millions of civilizations. The galaxy should be buzzing — which sharpens the Fermi paradox: so where is everybody?

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the intelligence fraction f_i down low.
lessons_data.insight: Make any single factor tiny and N collapses toward one — just us. The equation's real lesson is how little we know, not what the answer is.

glossary_data.tooltip: f_l — fraction of worlds where life starts
f_i — fraction that become intelligent
L — how long a civilisation broadcasts

title: Friedmann Equation
author: Alexander Friedmann
description: How the whole universe expands — and what its fate will be.
hook: Will the universe expand forever, or collapse in a Big Crunch? The Friedmann equation links the expansion rate to how much stuff the universe contains.
hook_action: Drag the cosmic density and the curvature.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the energy density ρ upward.
lessons_data.insight: More density means stronger gravity pulling against the expansion. Density and curvature together decide whether expansion wins or loses.

lessons_data.instruction: Set high density with positive curvature (Closed preset).
lessons_data.hint: Drag ρ high and k to +1.
lessons_data.insight: Enough density curves space closed — gravity eventually halts and reverses the expansion into a Big Crunch. The universe's geometry is its destiny.

lessons_data.instruction: Now set curvature k to 0.
lessons_data.insight: A perfectly flat universe sits on the knife-edge between expanding forever and collapsing. Measurements say ours is astonishingly close to exactly flat.

glossary_data.tooltip: ρ — the matter and energy density
k — the geometry of space
Sets how fast the universe grows

title: Matrix Multiplication
author: Arthur Cayley
description: Chaining two transformations into one.
hook: Rotate an image, then scale it — matrix multiplication fuses those two steps into a single operation. It's the engine behind graphics, neural nets, and search rankings.
hook_action: Drag the matrix dimension and feel the cost grow.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the matrix dimension n upward.
lessons_data.insight: Each output entry is a dot product of a row and a column. An n×n product needs about n³ multiplications.

lessons_data.instruction: Push n to its maximum.
lessons_data.insight: That n³ cost is why multiplying large matrices dominates the runtime of training neural networks — and why faster matrix-multiply algorithms are worth millions.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag n back down and think about order.
lessons_data.insight: Matrix multiplication isn't commutative: AB usually differs from BA. Rotating then scaling is not the same as scaling then rotating — order is meaning.

glossary_data.tooltip: Row i dotted with column j gives entry (i,j)
n — only matched inner dimensions can multiply
Each output entry is one dot product

title: Eigenvalue Equation
author: David Hilbert
description: The special directions a transformation only stretches.
hook: Most vectors get rotated when you apply a matrix. A precious few only get stretched, never turned — those eigenvectors reveal the true axes of a transformation.
hook_action: Drag the eigenvalue to stretch, shrink, or flip the eigenvector.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the eigenvalue λ upward.
lessons_data.insight: Along an eigenvector, the matrix acts like simple multiplication by λ — pure stretching, no rotation. λ is the stretch factor.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag λ between 0 and 1.
lessons_data.insight: An eigenvalue below 1 shrinks that direction. Repeatedly applying the matrix makes those components fade — which is exactly how systems settle toward a steady state.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag λ negative.
lessons_data.insight: A negative eigenvalue flips the eigenvector to point the opposite way. Eigenvalues run everything from PageRank to the vibration modes of a bridge.

glossary_data.tooltip: λ — the factor a vector is scaled by
A direction the matrix leaves unrotated
Av = λv — pure stretch, no turn

title: Determinant (2×2)
author: Gottfried Leibniz
description: How much a transformation scales area — and whether it's reversible.
hook: A matrix can stretch, squash, or flip space. The determinant is the single number telling you how much area it scales — and a determinant of zero means it crushes space flat.
hook_action: Drag the matrix entries and watch the determinant change.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the entry a and watch ad − bc change.
lessons_data.insight: The determinant is the area-scaling factor of the transformation. Bigger magnitude means the unit square is stretched into a larger parallelogram.

lessons_data.instruction: Try to make the determinant zero (Singular preset).
lessons_data.hint: Use the Singular preset, or set a·d = b·c.
lessons_data.insight: When ad equals bc, the determinant is zero: the transformation flattens 2D space onto a line. Such a matrix has no inverse — information is irretrievably lost.

lessons_data.instruction: Now make d negative (a reflection).
lessons_data.insight: A negative determinant means the transformation flips orientation — like a mirror. The sign tells you whether space was reflected, the size tells you by how much it grew.

glossary_data.tooltip: ad − bc — the area-scaling factor
How the matrix scales a unit area
A zero determinant means non-invertible

title: Singular Value Decomposition
author: Eugenio Beltrami
description: Break any matrix into rotation, stretch, and rotation.
hook: Every matrix, no matter how messy, is secretly just a rotation, then a stretch along clean axes, then another rotation. That decomposition powers image compression and recommendation engines.
hook_action: Drag the singular values to keep or discard information.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the second singular value σ₂ down.
lessons_data.insight: Singular values rank directions by importance. Shrinking the small ones loses little — most of the matrix's structure lives in the largest few.

lessons_data.instruction: Drive σ₂ to nearly zero while σ₁ stays large.
lessons_data.insight: Throwing away tiny singular values is lossy compression: a photo or dataset rebuilt from just the top few looks almost identical at a fraction of the size.

lessons_data.instruction: Now set both singular values roughly equal.
lessons_data.hint: Drag σ₂ back up near σ₁.
lessons_data.insight: When all singular values matter, nothing can be discarded — the matrix is genuinely full-rank. SVD is the math behind PCA, latent semantic analysis, and Netflix-style recommenders.

glossary_data.tooltip: σ — the strength of each component
The number of non-zero singular values
Dropping small σ compresses the data

title: Dot Product
author: Josiah Willard Gibbs
description: How much two vectors point the same way.
hook: Search engines, recommendation systems, and neural networks all ask the same question billions of times: how similar are these two vectors? The dot product is the answer.
hook_action: Drag the angle between the vectors and their lengths.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the angle θ between the vectors.
lessons_data.insight: The dot product follows the cosine of the angle: largest when the vectors align, shrinking as they diverge.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the angle to 90°.
lessons_data.insight: At a right angle, cos(90°) = 0, so the dot product vanishes. A zero dot product is the definition of perpendicular — the test for orthogonality everywhere in math.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the angle to 0°.
lessons_data.insight: Perfectly aligned vectors give the maximum dot product. Cosine similarity uses exactly this to measure how alike two documents, songs, or word-embeddings are.

glossary_data.tooltip: |a| — the length of a vector
θ — the angle between the two vectors
Measures how much one vector lies along another

title: Cross Product
author: Josiah Willard Gibbs
description: A vector perpendicular to two others — and the area they span.
hook: Turn a wrench: the force and the handle define a twisting axis pointing straight out. The cross product produces that perpendicular vector — torque, magnetism, and 3D normals all rely on it.
hook_action: Drag the angle between the vectors and their lengths.

lessons_data.instruction: Drag the angle θ between the vectors.
lessons_data.insight: The cross product's magnitude follows the sine of the angle — the exact opposite of the dot product. It measures the area of the parallelogram the vectors span.

lessons_data.instruction: Set the angle to 90°.
lessons_data.insight: At a right angle, sin(90°) = 1 and the cross product is largest. This maximum is why torque is greatest when you push a wrench perpendicular to the handle.

lessons_data.instruction: Now drag the angle to 0°.
lessons_data.insight: Parallel vectors span no area, so their cross product is zero. The result also points perpendicular to both inputs — which is how 3D graphics compute surface normals for lighting.

glossary_data.tooltip: |a| — the length of a vector
θ — the angle between the two vectors
The result points perpendicular to both
